approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would update the rules for Commonwealth legislative instruments, building on recommendations from a 2008 review.
It would change how these instruments are registered, scrutinised, and automatically repealed, and improve the public register of them.
The bill would also create administrative efficiencies and make Commonwealth laws easier for the public to access.
The bill would implement outstanding recommendations from the 2008 review of the Legislative Instruments Act 2003.
It would make other changes to improve how Commonwealth Acts and instruments are written and managed.
The bill would also contribute to the government's deregulation agenda by making government operations more efficient and laws more accessible.
Commonwealth rule-makers, agencies, and the public who access Commonwealth laws.

Introduced the Acts and Instruments (Framework Reform) Bill 2014 to consolidate Commonwealth acts and legislative instruments into a single Federal Register of Legislation, building on a 2008 statutory review of the Legislative Instruments Act, which came into force in 2005, that drew more than 60 stakeholder responses, and noted the government's Repeal Days had already removed over 10,000 spent legislative instruments this year.

Supported the Acts and Instruments (Framework Reform) Bill, explaining it implements recommendations from a 2008 statutory review led by Anthony Blunn, Ian Govey and Professor John McMillan, merging the Acts Publication Act 1905 and the Legislative Instruments Act 2003 into a single Federal Register of Legislation.

Discussed the Acts and Instruments (Framework Reform) Bill, noting the Legislative Instruments Act will be renamed the Legislation Act, and highlighted Australia's reputation for plain-English legal drafting, citing Australian-drafted telecommunications access provisions adopted by Malaysia's communications regulator.

Supported passage of the Acts and Instruments (Framework Reform) Bill 2014, saying it would align Commonwealth legislative frameworks, improve access to justice, create administrative efficiencies and reduce red tape.

Reported that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights had examined 250 bills and 1,717 instruments during 2014, finding 213 bills and 1,707 instruments compatible with human rights, and highlighted the committee's scrutiny of four national security bills as its most challenging work of the year.
